conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is to listen, not to judge, and to help you feel supported as you navigate these early weeks with your baby.

We’re going to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied set of ten questions that helps us understand how motherhood has been feeling for you emotionally over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it simply flags any signs of depression or anxiety so we can offer the right help.

Everything you share is confidential. If you ever mention thoughts of harming yourself, I’ll work with you right away to keep you safe, but otherwise our conversation stays between us unless you choose otherwise.

I’ll ask each question in everyday language—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you answer, just tell me whatever best describes your recent experience. Ready to start?

First question: Over the last seven days, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to—little pleasures like a warm drink, a song on the radio, or a friend’s text? Or has that enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly… not really. I’ll catch maybe a tiny flicker of enjoyment if a song I used to love comes on, but it feels muted—like I’m hearing it from another room. Most of the time I just think, “What’s the point?” and go back to staring at the baby monitor or folding onesies.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve laughed a couple of times—like when my husband made that silly face trying to get the baby to burp—but even then the laugh felt kind of forced, like I had to remind myself it was supposed to be funny. Mostly I just feel flat, like the humor’s buried under a heavy blanket.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—like our weekly coffee run or even just a shower without interruptions—but now it all feels like another chore on the list. Sometimes I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow will be better,” but the actual looking-forward feeling just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby spits up right after I feed him, I instantly think I must’ve over-fed him or held him wrong. When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. last night, I kept replaying everything I did—maybe I ate something that bothered him, maybe I’m just not calming him right. I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilt still swoops in every time something feels off.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep and totally fine, but my heart’s racing like something awful is about to happen—SIDS, choking, the crib collapsing… I check the monitor a dozen times an hour. I can’t point to any real danger, but the worry just parks itself in my chest and won’t leave.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. It hits out of nowhere—like yesterday, I was just warming a bottle and suddenly felt this wave of terror, heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. I knew nothing was wrong, but my body felt like the house was on fire. It passed after a few minutes, but those spells keep catching me off guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Even simple stuff—folding a load of onesies or answering a text—feels like climbing a mountain. I’ll look around at the mess and think, “I’ll never dig out,” then just sit there frozen while the baby naps. I manage the basics, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. After the night feeds I lie there staring at the ceiling, mind racing—did I burp him long enough, is he breathing, am I already failing him? It can take an hour to drift off, then I jolt awake at every tiny grunt over the monitor. By morning I feel like I’ve barely slept at all.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears start welling up for no clear reason. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—he’s healthy, I’m not alone,” but the miserable feeling doesn’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week. Yesterday I just looked at the pile of laundry and burst into tears—couldn’t stop for almost ten minutes. It felt like everything was crashing down, even though it was just clothes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind. Just brief flashes—like when I’m rocking him at 3 a.m. and feel totally useless—sometimes I picture stepping in front of a bus or taking too many pills, but I shake it off right away. I don’t want to die; I just want the ache to stop. I haven’t made any plans or done anything, and I don’t think I ever would, but the thoughts do pop up.

You have been coping with persistent low mood, daily anxiety and panic, overwhelming guilt about your baby care, and even brief thoughts of escape. <quote>I just want the ache to stop</quote> captures how exhausted and sad you feel. These symptoms have lasted most of the day, nearly every day, and are understandably making it hard to enjoy motherhood or manage everyday tasks.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter and a persistent flat mood, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('a lot', 'every time something feels off') matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, physiologically intense anxiety without identifiable triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Response describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-constant overwhelm ('Most of the time') and inability to manage routine tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with spontaneous tearfulness, indicating sadness occurs "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two crying episodes in a week triggered by minor stressors, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intrusive self-harm ideas ("crossed my mind," "brief flashes") occurring in specific moments, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus Item 10 ≥1 indicates high risk per EPDS guidelines. You describe core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest (<sym>no looking-forward feeling</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and recurrent thoughts of death. These have persisted for more than two weeks and cause clinically significant distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med>, psychiatrist, or local perinatal mental-health team
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you until professional help is in place
3. Call your local 24-h crisis line if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
5. Plan small, achievable daily goals-one shower, one walk, one nutritious snack-to counteract the overwhelm
6. Practise 4-7-8 breathing when panic surges: inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s
7. Limit monitor-checking to once per hour to reduce <sym>nocturnal anxiety</sym>; place baby on back in clear cot, no loose bedding, to address SIDS worries safely
8. Share this screening summary with your partner or family so they can support appointments and household tasks
9. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms:  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Daily, unprovoked anxiety, panic spells, intrusive catastrophic worries (SIDS, harm)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia unrelated to infant needs  
- Overwhelm, psychomotor fatigue (“frozen,” tasks feel mountainous)  
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation (no plan or intent)

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 weeks; cause subjective impairment and distress.

Risk flags:  
1. Active suicidal ideation (passive, no plan) – safety concern  
2. Significant anxiety/panic overlay suggesting possible comorbid postpartum anxiety  
3. Functional impairment (self-care, household tasks) and infant-care worries

Screening impression: High clinical likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; immediate safety assessment and follow-up evaluation recommended.
